clinicalPearls: Retained placenta is failure to deliver the placenta within a defined interval after birth, commonly thirty minutes with active management of the third stage or up to an hour with physiological management

Three broad mechanisms are recognised: a separated placenta trapped behind a closed cervix (trapped placenta), a placenta that fails to separate because of inadequate uterine contraction (placenta adherens), and a morbidly adherent placenta of the accreta spectrum
It is an important cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage, both because the uterus cannot contract effectively around retained tissue and because partial separation opens maternal sinuses

Risk factors include a previous retained placenta, previous uterine surgery or curettage, preterm delivery, placenta praevia, and grand multiparity; abnormal placentation should be considered when the uterus is scarred

Initial steps are to ensure the bladder is empty, encourage breastfeeding or nipple stimulation, give a uterotonic, and attempt controlled cord traction; injudicious traction risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion
If these measures fail, manual removal of the placenta under regional or general anaesthesia is required, with antibiotic cover and careful assessment for completeness
If the placenta cannot be separated and morbid adherence is evident, forced removal must be avoided; senior help and preparation for major haemorrhage and possible hysterectomy are needed
After delivery of the placenta, examine it for completeness, since retained fragments can cause ongoing or secondary haemorrhage and endometritis
reference.pathophysiology: Normal placental separation depends on brisk contraction and retraction of the myometrium after delivery of the fetus, which shears the placenta from the decidua basalis along the plane of the spongy layer and then closes off the underlying spiral arteries. Retention arises when this sequence fails. In placenta adherens, poor and often localised myometrial contraction prevents shearing, so the placenta remains attached. In a trapped placenta, the placenta separates but the cervix contracts down before expulsion, imprisoning it. In placenta accreta spectrum, deficient decidua, typically over a scar, allows chorionic villi to invade the myometrium so that no cleavage plane exists. Because retained tissue prevents the uterus from contracting fully, the exposed vascular placental bed continues to bleed, linking retained placenta closely with postpartum haemorrhage.
additionalDifferentials: Placenta adherens due to uterine atony
Trapped or incarcerated placenta behind a constriction ring or closed cervix
A succenturiate lobe left in situ
Uterine inversion presenting as failure to deliver the placenta
A constriction ring or hourglass contraction from mismanaged third stage
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of blood loss, uterine tone, and maternal haemodynamic status
Full blood count and group-and-save or crossmatch, with coagulation studies if bleeding is heavy
Examination of the delivered placenta and membranes for completeness
Bedside ultrasound to assess for retained tissue and features suggesting abnormal placentation
Review of antenatal imaging for placenta accreta spectrum when the placenta will not separate over a scar
Observations and inflammatory markers if delayed retention presents with suspected endometritis
redFlags: Heavy or continuing postpartum bleeding with the placenta still undelivered
Inability to separate the placenta with suspicion of accreta spectrum
Uterine inversion, with sudden pain, haemorrhage, and a mass at or beyond the introitus
Fever and offensive lochia suggesting infected retained tissue
reference.prognosis: With prompt uterotonics, bladder emptying, and timely manual removal, most cases resolve without lasting harm; delay increases the risk of major haemorrhage, and cases complicated by placenta accreta spectrum carry a significant risk of massive haemorrhage and hysterectomy.
pitfalls: Applying vigorous cord traction against a poorly contracted uterus, causing cord avulsion or uterine inversion
Failing to empty the bladder, which impedes uterine contraction and placental delivery
Persisting with attempts at manual removal when placenta accreta is evident
Not inspecting the placenta for missing cotyledons or a succenturiate lobe
Underestimating cumulative blood loss and delaying escalation
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on postpartum haemorrhage
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Begin with simple measures: empty the bladder, encourage breastfeeding or nipple stimulation, give a uterotonic such as oxytocin, and attempt gentle controlled cord traction, avoiding forceful traction that risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion
Perform manual removal of the placenta under regional or general anaesthesia when initial measures fail, checking the specimen for completeness
Give antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of manual removal
Manage associated postpartum haemorrhage with intravenous access, fluid resuscitation, uterotonics, tranexamic acid and crossmatched blood as needed
Suspect placenta accreta spectrum when the placenta will not separate over a uterine scar, and prepare for possible hysterectomy
Escalate promptly to senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams, with interventional radiology or specialist input for morbidly adherent placentation
